The Vaelith is solitary and amphibious. It spends the bright hours of the long day resting in shade or shallow water, then becomes active at dusk and through the night. Pods will mob a predator together, striking with wings and tentacles. Symbiotic flying crustaceans live on their skin, eating parasites and cleaning wounds.

The Ythrian Cloud Mantle is a keystone species. It controls aeroplankton and sky-swift populations, disperses spores across continents, and transports nutrients from sky to sea when it dies. Its gas bladders release methane, influencing atmospheric chemistry. An adult Veilwing is roughly the size of a small aircraft: 9–12 meters from fin tip to fin tip, with a central body 2–3 meters long. It looks like a cross between a manta ray, a zeppelin, and a jellyfish.

The sac is filled mostly with methane and hydrogen produced by symbiotic microbes in the creature’s gut, giving the Veilwing near-neutral buoyancy. Through the translucent skin, you can see branching veins and slow-moving internal fluids. The sac pulses gently as the animal adjusts its lift.

Below the sac is a spindle-shaped body covered in rubbery, slate-violet skin. The skin is patterned with faint bioluminescent spots that shift from amber to blue depending on mood and health. The creature has two enormous lateral fins—thin membranes stretched over flexible cartilage struts—that undulate slowly to steer and ride thermals. Four smaller ventral fins act as stabilizers. At the front is a wide, scoop-like mouth fringed with stiff baleen bristles and fine cilia. Four eyes sit on short stalks: two large forward-facing eyes adapted to dim red-orange light, and two smaller dorsal eyes that watch for predators above. Six long sensory tendrils trail behind the body, tasting the air and detecting pressure changes. Two shorter ventral tendrils can coil and grip floating debris or anchor the animal during storms.

The Veilwing is a slow, communal grazer. It spends most of its life drifting at 20–40 km/h along the terminator winds, following blooms of aeroplankton. Symbiotic microbes in its gut break down tough spore coats and cellulose-like films, releasing methane that the Veilwing stores in its gas sac. This means feeding directly helps it stay aloft.

It changes altitude by inflating or venting its gas sac. To rise, it accumulates methane and spreads its fins wide. The Veilwing’s main predators are “dive-hawks,” slender six-winged animals that stoop from higher clouds. Older Veilwings that lose buoyancy often sink slowly to the lower cloud deck, where their bodies are consumed by drifting decomposers—returning nutrients to the aerial ecosystem.
